newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Rates fall as S.Africa shortage hits two-month low.
newsitem.headline: Rates fall as S.Africa shortage hits two-month low.

text.p: South African money market rates edged lower on Thursday as the shortage moved to its lowest level in over two months.

The "big four" banks all quoted their three-month NCDs rates at 16.55 percent offered from between 16.60 to 16.65 percent previously after the Reserve Bank reported the shortage fell to 7.853 billion rand on Wednesday from 8.411 billion rand.
A central bank official said the shortage was at its lowest level since February 8 when it touched 7.876 billion rand.

"The shortage has been fairly low this week and has now gone below eight billion rand. As a result call rates might go lower today, which pulls the asset rates down," Andre Pretorius, chief money market trader at Securities Investment Bank said.
He said call rates were currently steady at around 16.00 to 16.25 percent.

Roelf du Plooy, assistant general manager in the Reserve Bank's money and capital market division, said the decline in the shortage had come about as a result of a slight mismatch in government flows.

"The main reason was that government expenditure was a little bit more than we expected it to be, so we withdrew less money from the Tax and Loan accounts than the actual amount that was spent," du Plooy said.
He said the shortage could be expected to tick up again on Thursday. "It depends on what the forex moves do today, but if that stays the same then I would expect it to increase again a little bit."
He said the shortage's recent fall to below 10 billion rand, where it has held steadily for the last two months, was largely as a result as a hefty fall in notes and coins.
Notes and coins in circulation had decreased by about three billion rand since the beginning of the month, he said. They stood at 18.441 billion rand Wednesday.
"We are also seeing an inflow of foreign exchange which will also contribute to the lower shortage," du Plooy said.

Money market traders said that the sentiment on the money market had also been boosted by renewed optimism on the long end, where the yield on the R150 has fallen from around 15.30 percent at the beginning of the week to 15.05 percent on Thursday
"Sentiment is positive on the back of the gilts which is spilling over into the money market," Pretorius said.
"There is no negative news in the money market...it is drifting sideways to maybe just a touch bullish," Pretorius added.
